blurb: Massive Hungarian flock guardian wearing the heaviest corded white coat of any dog
description: The Komondor is a large Hungarian livestock guardian with a long, corded white coat that looks like a mop, described as calm at home and fearless in defence.
answer: The Komondor, also called the Hungarian sheepdog, is a large livestock guardian from Hungary, famous for its long white corded coat that resembles a mop. Females are at least about 65 cm and males at least about 70 cm tall, weighing roughly 40 to 60 kg, and the breed is described as calm, independent and fiercely protective.

body: The Komondor was brought to Hungary by the Cumans, a nomadic Turkic-speaking people who settled there in the 12th and 13th centuries; the name is thought to mean Cuman dog. The breed is believed to descend from Tibetan dogs, and Komondor remains have been found in Cuman graves. It is first mentioned in writing in a Hungarian codex of 1544.

Many Komondors were killed during World War II. The breed has since been declared a Hungarian national treasure and is fairly common in Hungary today. It is related to the Puli and the South Russian Ovcharka, but developed separately from the other Hungarian guardian, the Kuvasz.

The Komondor is robust and strongly muscled, slightly longer than tall, with a broad head and black nose and lips. Standards give minimum heights with no upper limit. Its white coat, about 20 to 27 cm long, is said to be the heaviest in the canine world. The soft puppy coat combines with the coarser outer coat to form cords over about two years, and the cords need some separating by hand. Once the cords form, moulting is minimal.

Like most livestock guardians, the Komondor is described as calm and steady in normal conditions but fearless in defending its charges. It was bred to think and act independently. It is said to be affectionate and gentle with its family and protective of household pets, wary of strangers and intolerant of trespassing animals. It tends to rest by day and patrol its territory at night.

The breed is described as unsuited to apartment life. The corded coat needs regular attention to prevent it matting into one mass, can look off-white if not washed, and takes about two and a half days to dry after a bath.
The source text does not describe specific health conditions in the Komondor. Breed clubs generally recommend health screening of breeding stock and regular veterinary check-ups.

faq.a: Once the cords have fully formed, moulting is minimal; the main shedding happens in puppyhood before the cords develop.

faq.q: How big does a Komondor get?
faq.a: It is a large breed: females are at least about 65 cm and males at least about 70 cm at the withers, weighing roughly 40 to 60 kg.

faq.q: Is the Komondor recognised by the FCI?
faq.a: Yes. The FCI lists it as breed number 53 in Group 1, with Hungary as the country of origin.
